thread: Data mining, SIGIR-style search, recommendation, and web learning all solve the same plain problem: a system has far more possible evidence than it can inspect, and far more possible answers than it can show. A search engine cannot read the whole web for every query. A recommender cannot ask a person to rate every item. A fraud detector cannot manually inspect every account. A language agent cannot try every tool path. The shared mathematical move is to turn messy behavior into structured comparisons: what is near what, what should be ranked above what, what caused what, what evidence should receive weight, and what uncertainty remains. The families differ by surface task, but the core pressure is the same: make a defensible decision from partial, biased, noisy, changing evidence.
arc: The family map is the easiest way to see the field. SIGIR and information-retrieval papers start with matching: a query, document, user, item, or answer must be represented so relevance can be scored and ranked. Recommender and advertising papers add allocation pressure: the system must choose not only what matches, but what to spend attention, budget, or exposure on. Graph-learning and knowledge-graph papers treat links as evidence; meaning spreads through neighbors, paths, communities, and relations. Causal-inference papers ask a stricter question: if we changed this action, ranking, subsidy, exposure, or answer, what outcome would actually move? Trust, fairness, misinformation, privacy, and security papers ask what can go wrong when the score is optimized blindly: hidden bias, leakage, manipulation, confounding, or unsafe content. LLM, RAG, and agent papers reuse the same machinery at a larger interface: retrieve evidence, rank candidate passages or tools, focus attention, and optimize behavior from feedback. Efficiency papers sit underneath all of them because the best mathematical idea fails if it cannot run at web scale. Across these families, the recurring concepts form a ladder: measure information, estimate probabilities, place meaning in a space, spread evidence through a network, rank by a learned score, follow sequences through time, focus on relevant pieces, separate cause from coincidence, and optimize the settings that reduce measured wrongness.
punchline: The important concept behind the math is not that everything becomes a neural model. It is that every family needs a reason to ignore most possibilities without throwing away the answer. Similarity says nearby things can stand in for each other. Ranking says exact values matter less than order. Probability says repeated evidence can estimate future chances. Attention says a few pieces of context can dominate a decision. Network propagation says neighbors carry useful information. Causal reasoning says action requires more than correlation. Optimization says a measured error can guide improvement. Learning from examples ties these together by discovering the space, weights, score, or policy when humans cannot write it down. That is the consistency with SIGGRAPH: different world, same discipline. Preserve the relationships that make the object real, compress what repeats, score what is wrong, and state when the shortcut can be trusted.
